articles.title_orig: Four tankers struck by explosions in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
articles.title_zh: Four tankers struck by explosions in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
articles.content_orig:
Since the US war on Iran began in February, there have been hundreds of oil spills, posing a ‘generational’ threat to wildlife
T he vast, dark slicks in the strait of Hormuz are visible from space. Throughout October, oil tankers were struck by missiles or sea mines in the waterway and spilled crude into the sea. The pollution has spread across the Gulf, contaminating coastlines and threatening to cause lasting damage to marine ecosystems that are home to dolphins, sea turtles and countless species of fish.
Eight months into the war between the US and Iran, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes has become a battlefield and the centre of a growing environmental disaster .
The naval blockade of the strait has made documenting the pollution from on the ground almost impossible. But analysis of satellite images, combined with the testimony of environmental experts and marine biologists, can help build up a picture.
The strait of Hormuz, the only maritime passage between the Gulf and the Arabian Sea, is home to a rich but fragile marine environment including coral reefs, mangrove forests and seagrass meadows that support a wealth of marine life.
It plays a vital role in the circulation of water and nutrients and serves as a migration route for marine mammals. Even in peacetime, its ecosystems have faced mounting pressure from shipping, oil extraction and coastal development.
Oil can coat birds’ feathers, making it difficult for them to float and find food. It can cover mangrove roots, preventing the trees from absorbing oxygen and potentially killing them.
Bernhard Riegl, a marine biologist at Nova Southeastern University in Florida, who has studied the Gulf for more than 30 years, warned that the war could cause lasting damage to its confined waters, already under severe pressure from the climate crisis.
“Since the Gulf is shallow, and summer is the least windy period of the year, atmospheric heat is rapidly translated into ocean heat. That heat kills corals, algae, fishes. There is no cold, deep water that could mix and buffer this heat,” Riegl said.
“Everybody knows that oil in water is not good. The potential for additional damage is significant. There is no such thing as a ‘clean war’. Not for the unlucky humans that are drawn into it, nor for the unlucky environment in which the conflict takes place.”
Since the war began on 28 February, Greenpeace has identified more than 500 instances of oil spills through satellite monitoring across the Gulf, the strait of Hormuz and the Arabian Sea. The findings include major spills linked to attacks on vessels, as well as others detected around the time of strikes but whose origins could not be confirmed.
“Adding together the daily mapped footprints [of the spills] gives a cumulative total of approximately 20,000 square kilometres – almost the size of Wales,” said Nina Noelle, a Greenpeace expert on environmental disaster relief.
More than 133 attacks on oil tankers have taken place since the beginning of the conflict, according to Greenpeace. October was the worst month, with more than 30 confirmed or reported attacks in the strait of Hormuz and surrounding waters, according to the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. The attacks have continued into November.
Among the most polluting of the October attacks was a strike on the supertanker Gem No 2 off the coast of the United Arab Emirates, which left a slick stretching more than 21 miles (35km). A satellite image dated 19 October shows a huge patch of black moving into the clear waters off the coast of Umm Al Quwain.
Greenpeace estimates that an attack on a tanker in early June resulted in a slick off the coast of Oman that covered more than 600 sq km (230 sq miles) at its peak. Two Iranian naval vessels hit in March continued leaking oil for months, said Wim Zwijnenburg, an environmental researcher with the Dutch peace organisation Pax.
An attack on the Liberian-flagged Minoan Pioneer on 3 August has also been linked to a major slick.
Oil pollution has reached several coastlines since the war began. In March, a slick from the Shahid Bagheri was detected near the Hara mangroves. In April, pollution threatened the protected Shidvar Island, home to coral reefs, seabirds and turtles. Oil was also reported washing ashore at Qeshm Island in August, near important fishing grounds and turtle nesting sites.
after newsletter promotion
Satellite imagery also shows slicks near Oman’s Musandam national park and Iran’s Minab River delta , two areas rich in wildlife. Musandam is home to coral reefs and seabird breeding grounds, while the Minab delta has protected mudflats and forests of mangroves.
Environmental organisations are continuing to analyse satellite imagery but warn that the full extent of the damage cannot be established without investigations on the ground, which remain extremely difficult. Some of the researchers and environmentalists contacted for comment in Iran and Gulf states said they had been instructed by domestic authorities not to speak publicly about the environmental damage caused by the war.
Establishing responsibility is not straightforward, but Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has been blamed for most of the attacks. US forces have also targeted tankers, disabling Iranian vessels attempting to cross a US naval blockade and striking others in response to Iranian missile attacks on US warships.
According to a Wall Street Journal report , the largest oil spill was caused by a strike carried out by the UAE’s air force on oil storage tanks on Lavan Island. The strikes resulted in crude oil flushing into the Gulf and affecting coastal areas, including the nearby nature reserves of Shidvar Island.
In some instances, countries bordering the strait have responded to spills. After the attack on the Gem No 2, for instance, the UAE closed beaches, launched a major cleanup and monitored its desalination plants. Authorities said on 30 October that the leak had been stopped and pollution was declining.
In Oman , divers and equipment were deployed to a damaged vessel and crews cleared oil from 7 miles of coastline near the Hallaniyat Islands.
But the wider environmental damage may prove far harder to contain. “Oil could remain trapped in sediments, shorelines and mangrove roots long after slicks disappear, damaging marine food chains and threatening coastal communities dependent on fishing,” Noelle said.
Contamination can affect organisms ranging from small invertebrates to fish, birds and turtles. “Mangroves and coral reefs can take decades to recover, particularly when oil persists in sediments,” she added. “Repeated spills, such as those in the strait of Hormuz, risk worsening the damage.”
Riegl said the aftermath of the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s and the first Gulf war, when tankers, loading facilities and oilfields were targeted, provided evidence of the lasting impact of large-scale oil pollution on Gulf ecosystems.
A 2020 study traced widespread deposits of tar – the thick, sticky residue left as crude oil breaks down – on Qatari beaches to the Gulf war. A study in 2022 found sediment on Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island still contaminated by oil from the 1983-85 Nowruz spills during the Iran-Iraq war, which collectively leaked 80m gallons of crude into the sea.
Riegl said: “Any organism that has to dig into beaches [affected by spills], like sea turtles when they lay eggs, will encounter the contaminated strata and adverse effects can be expected. Burrowing organisms like ghost crabs will continue to bring contaminated material to the surface.
“Clearly, the effects of large-scale oil pollution remain detectable for decades – so this is a generational problem. We could really lose something irreplaceable.”

articles.title_orig: Stocks Slide on Nvidia Troubles, Oil Edges Lower: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Slide on Nvidia Troubles, Oil Edges Lower: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s shares plummeted Thursday, sending tremors through global markets, as the company’s chief executive, Jensen Huang , stepped down from his role.
Shares in Nvidia dropped as much as 14 percent when markets opened for trading on Thursday, extending a decline that has wiped out more than $1 trillion from the company’s market value this month alone. The stock began to reverse most of its losses by late morning.
The broader market rose slightly, too, as investors began to conclude that the fallout of Mr. Jensen’s departure would not fundamentally undermine the artificial intelligence trade. Yields on the 10-year U.S. Treasury rose above 5 percent on Thursday for the first time in weeks. Yields go up when Treasury prices go down.
Nvidia has emerged as central to the A.I. economy because its chips — or graphic processing units — help train and power models across the industry. It has also become a central bank of sorts for several A.I. companies, because its finances are deeply intertwined with those of everyone from frontier A.I. labs to neoclouds, which rent out computing power.
“This is an Nvidia problem before it is an A.I. problem,” said Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial. But he added that Nvidia’s woes could trickle through to other companies.
“Where I would be careful is with the smaller A.I. cloud companies that leaned on Nvidia’s checkbook,” he said. “If the new regime gets more conservative about financing its own customers, that is where it shows up first.”

It's Xbox's 25th anniversary this month, and Microsoft is announcing a variety of new "stuff" over the course of the week.
First up, we have a shiny new feature I know some of you have been passionate about, dubbed Xbox Playback .
Last year, it felt like almost every brand on Earth did some form of "Spotify Wrapped," which showcased what music and podcasting habits you had throughout the year. Even my banking app had a "Wrapped" last year, but Xbox was conspicuously absent from the festivities. I wrote back then that it was because they were working on something bigger , something that would be future-proofed, and it seems we now know what it is.
Announced today on Xbox Wire , Xbox Playback is a "personalized experience" that mimics previous anniversary data collections Xbox has done, although, from what I've heard, it will be available annually too moving forward.
To see your Xbox Playback, head over here and sign in with your account, or head to your Playback Archive to explore more of your history.
XBOX Playback starts rolling out now. It's a look at what you played, who you played with, and what you accomplished on XBOX over the last 25 years. https://t.co/HX5nOWldiX November 12, 2026
"XBOX is introducing XBOX Playback, a new personalized experience that lets players revisit their gaming history across 25 years of XBOX," Microsoft said. "Players can discover their first XBOX game, most-played titles, total playtime, achievements, longest gaming streaks and other milestones. Playback will be accessible on console and the web, with personalized videos and shareable cards, rolling out gradually throughout the day in 15 countries." (..)
"Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Colombia, France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Mexico, Poland, South Africa, Spain, UK and US. Requires at least 1 XBOX Gamerscore, 1 achievement, and 1 minute of qualifying gameplay linked to your Xbox profile; access on console requires at least 1 minute of qualifying gameplay on console . Based on available data; some data may be incomplete or delayed."
It's a bit of a shame it's only available in 15 countries and not the total scope of Xbox's user base.. I'm pretty sure things like Spotify Wrapped are available to all customers. To speculate, Microsoft is pretty meticulous when it comes to regional data laws owing to its enterprise cloud division, and national rules it has to observe therein. I'll try and find out exactly why it's so limited in scope.
In any case, you can expect more Xbox 25th anniversary celebratory announcements throughout the day. I'm not expecting anything on the scale of an Xbox Helix reveal or Elder Scrolls 6 gameplay trailer, but could we finally see the Xbox Elite Controller Series 3 ? Here's hoping.

articles.title_orig: How Hamas shaped Gaza's winter flooding narrative before the first storm
articles.title_zh: How Hamas shaped Gaza's winter flooding narrative before the first storm
articles.content_orig:
“There was flooding in Gaza , but the narrative and scale of suffering was written by Hamas before it even started raining,” Justin Pozmanter, News Director at HonestReporting, told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
Pozmanter shared an exclusive report with the Post detailing how the Hamas-government winter campaign and a Hamas-run media office figure traveled from Telegram to the international press between November 1 and 10, 2026.
The story begins on November 1, when the Gaza Winter Emergency Committee, a Hamas-government body, issued its first press statement, posted on the GMO’s Telegram channel.
The committee announced the “2026-2027 Winter Preparedness and Response Plan” and the national campaign “Together Towards a Safe Winter.” The release predicted a harsh, early winter and blamed Israeli restrictions on heavy machinery, spare parts, fuel, and shelter supplies.
It also provided a list of figures: 200,000 worn-out tents and one million tarps needed; 7,800 tents in dangerous locations; 2,000 cracked buildings at risk of collapse; and 70% of municipalities’ basic operating equipment destroyed.
Days later, on November 5, before any storm in the region, Euro-Med Monitor published an article named “Israel weaponizes cold weather against Palestinians in Gaza for fourth year, continues to ban shelter supplies.”
Many of the article’s claims can be traced directly back to the November 1 Hamas press release. For example, the article writes “Israel continues to deprive Palestinians in the Gaza Strip of safe shelter for the fourth consecutive year.” It then lists the same figures that appeared in the Hamas memo: 200,000 tents; one million tarps; 2,000 cracked buildings.
As HonestReporting noted, this was a pivot point.
The Hamas-aligned framing, such as “Israel is engineering a winter catastrophe,” was restated in the vocabulary of a human rights NGO, with figures sourced to a committee whose Hamas governance ties go unlabeled.
The first winter storm arrived on November 6, with footage of floods in Gaza circulating on social media.
A day later, on November 7 at 11:15 Israel time, roughly 12 hours after the first rain, the Hamas-run Government Media Office published a new press statement warning that “Within 12 hours: 70,000 tents flooded and $3 million in losses.”
It claimed dozens of walls collapsed, causing injuries, and warned that cracked buildings damaged in the “genocide war” may collapse, and holds Israel “fully responsible” for keeping crossings closed to shelter and reconstruction material. It also called on the international community and UN bodies to intervene.
Within a few hours, Reuters , the BBC, and NBC News began posting the “70,000 tents” figure. Reuters was the only one of the three that explicitly identified the GMO as Hamas-run.
Anti-Israel social media accounts then began amplifying the claims.
Drop Site News called it “deliberate and systematic cruelty... part of an effort to drive Palestinians out of Gaza... with full US support.”
Pro-Palestinian British doctor Rahmeh Aladwan said: “The Jewish occupation destroyed 82% of Gaza and has blocked caravans and building material for 3 years.”
Greta Thunberg posted on Facebook: “around 70,000 tents flooded... ISRAEL IS FULLY RESPONSIBLE. END THE GENOCIDE.”
HonestReporting also noted that the Hamas-run Gaza Government Media Office announced the 70,000-tent figure just hours after the rain began and already estimated losses at roughly three million dollars.
HonestReporting questioned how Hamas, in a matter of hours and during a downpour, definitively knew that 70,000 tents had been flooded.
In other countries, after a disaster strikes, it can take up to a few days for officials to even attain a preliminary estimate of the scope of the damage.
Few news sites mentioned the extensive preparations Israel went to make the Strip ready for bad weather.
Since September 4, 2026, roughly two months before the recent storm, COGAT (the Israeli Ministry of Defense body responsible for humanitarian coordination in Palestinian areas) has been posting on social media the steps it was taking in anticipation of the upcoming winter in the Gaza Strip.
This has included facilitating the entry of tents and shelter equipment, engine oil, generators and lights, medical equipment and supplies, tarpaulins, winter clothing, vacuum trucks, portable toilets, and spare vehicle parts.
By the time the storm arrived this past weekend, COGAT said that over 91,000 tents and 8,200 trucks full of winter necessities had entered the Gaza Strip since the beginning of the winterization campaign in September.
“COGAT will continue working in cooperation with the Board of Peace, the UN, international organizations, and the international community to maintain the humanitarian situation in the Gaza Strip at its current stable level ahead of the winter, while taking the necessary measures to prevent Hamas from seizing control of the humanitarian aid and essential supplies,” COGAT wrote on November 5.
As Pozmanter said, there was indeed flooding in Gaza, but the narrative and scale of suffering were written by Hamas before it even started raining.
“In their telling, parroted by affiliated organizations like Euro-med and largely trusted as fact by the press and many Western leaders, Israel was to blame, despite facilitating distribution of tens of thousands of tents and tons of winter gear to the population, something no other country has ever done for an enemy population during war,” he told the Post .
He also noted that, largely absent from the coverage, were any mentions that Hamas has “dismantled Israeli and donor-provided sewage and drainage systems and used the pipes to build rockets, and spent billions in international aid to build a vast tunnel network for themselves rather than infrastructure for their people.”
“The truth is, Hamas once again sacrificed Gazan civilians and the media, once again, demonstrated that it waives scrutiny when unverified accusations are leveled at Israel,” Pozmanter concluded.

articles.title_orig: The Bank of Nvidia just lost its banker — here’s where the AI trade is exposed
articles.title_zh: The Bank of Nvidia just lost its banker — here’s where the AI trade is exposed
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Jensen Huang didn't just sell chips for the AI boom. He helped pay for it, and Wall Street is now repricing everyone on his tab.
Huang resigned as Nvidia's ( NVDA ) CEO and left its board Thursday, effective immediately, after reports of two affairs , one involving an alleged Chinese spy. CFO Colette Kress is now interim CEO, and the company still plans to report earnings Tuesday.
Nvidia stock sank to its lowest level in more than a year, putting it briefly $2 trillion below its October record. But the selling hasn't hit the AI trade evenly . Nebius ( NBIS ) and CoreWeave ( CRWV ), cloud companies that rent out Nvidia chips, took the worst of it, while rivals Broadcom ( AVGO ) and AMD ( AMD ) and most of Big Tech held up.
That pattern traces the Bank of Nvidia .
Nvidia owns stakes in Intel ( INTC ), SpaceX ( SPCX ), CoreWeave, Coherent ( COHR ) and Safe Superintelligence, bought $3 billion of Meta's ( META ) stock offering, and has pledged up to $10 billion to Anthropic ahead of its IPO next week . It holds a $30 billion stake in OpenAI and has a preliminary deal to invest as much as $100 billion more. Many of those companies turn around and buy Nvidia's chips.
Nvidia's latest quarterly filing lists about $530 billion in commitments and guarantees, by Yahoo Finance's count, including roughly $65 billion to rent back cloud capacity from companies like CoreWeave and a guarantee of up to $105 billion on OpenAI's Ohio data center leases.
"It does bring into question what we've been talking about for ... the better part of the last year, which is a lot of these circular relationships," Liz Thomas, chief market strategist at SoFi, said at Yahoo Finance Invest .
The first is the dealmaker himself. Huang sat at the center of these deals, and Kress, who signed off on them as CFO, now decides how many more to write.
The OpenAI guarantee pays out only if OpenAI defaults, and the kind of downturn that would sink OpenAI would likely hit Nvidia's own sales at the same time.
Customers are paying slower too. Nvidia's receivables hit $63 billion last quarter, with bills taking about 60 days to collect, up from 45. Nvidia blamed longer terms on big deals.
And its own portfolio is shrinking. The value of Nvidia's largest public stock holdings has lost more than $20 billion in value since June, led by Intel.
The money behind the AI build-out was already getting harder to find. CoreWeave's CEO said this week the company won't borrow without collateral at today's high rates. BofA's Savita Subramanian told Yahoo Finance the tech giants are now selling more of their own stock than they buy back, saying they're "net issuers today rather than buying back their stock."
Nvidia's balance sheet is the counterweight, with about $99 billion in cash and securities against $33 billion of debt at the end of July.
Tuesday's earnings report will show whether Kress stands behind the guidance and the commitments, and whether customers are paying on time.
Thomas put the question for next week bluntly.
"Can the market survive without positive results from Nvidia?"

articles.title_orig: European leaders reject Russian push to overhaul continent’s security
articles.title_zh: European leaders reject Russian push to overhaul continent’s security
articles.content_orig:
Joe is based in Brussels, where he focuses on European politics and defence. He has covered the Ukraine war and its peace negotiations and reported on US elections from Washington DC
Britain and France should immediately deploy troops to Ukraine, a former head of Nato has said.
Anders Fogh Rasmussen accused Europe’s two nuclear powers of presiding over a “coalition of the waiting” while the Kremlin dragged out peace talks.
“For some months, France and the UK have tried to establish a coalition of the willing, but it’s more now a coalition of the waiting,” the 73-year-old former Danish prime minister told The Telegraph from his office in Brussels.
“We should transform that into a ‘coalition of the doing’ by deploying troops… you could not wait for a peace deal but actually push for peace by telling Putin ‘you cannot deter us, and we will help the Ukrainians defend against attacks against their critical infrastructure’.”
Mr Rasmussen’s call for action came during US-led negotiations in Abu Dhabi between Ukraine and Russia, which focused on security guarantees and preventing a future war.
European officials were kept out of the room after Moscow objected to their involvement in the two-day talks, which Ukraine described on Wednesday as “one of the toughest” negotiations yet.
Vladimir Medinsky, the head of the Russian delegation, said after the talks: “We have no idea what the Europeans are doing here, this is a trilateral meeting. They can hang out in the lobby if they want.”
Mr Rasmussen, who was Nato’s secretary-general between 2009 and 2014, believes that Europe must show Vladimir Putin that it is serious in its support for Ukraine, even as it continues to be denied a seat at the table.
He has devised a five-point strategy to stop the war and prevent Europe from “sleepwalking into a permanent war on the Continent”.
He called on Germany, Spain and Greece to empty their stockpiles of Patriot interceptors to help Kyiv protect itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks, and suggested Nato extends its integrated air and missile defence systems over western Ukraine to bolster defences.
On top of this, Mr Rasmussen said the EU should confiscate more than €200bn (£175bn) in frozen Russian assets and use them to top up Kyiv’s defence budget. The “Coalition of the Willing” should be overhauled to include only countries willing to go to war with Russia should it attack Ukraine after any ceasefire is negotiated, he added.
“President Trump has chosen Moscow and sided with Vladimir Putin,” Mr Rasmussen said. “So in Europe, we have a particular responsibility for helping Ukraine, and that’s why I call on European leaders to wake up.”
He added: “It’s clear that the Russians do not want peace. Putin has no incentives to engage in the peace negotiations as long as he believes he can succeed on the battlefield.
“So, we need to change his calculus, we need to put more pressure on Russia.”
His plan would involve French and British troops as a “reassurance force” to protect Ukraine’s population centres.
It would also free up more Ukrainian resources to commit to the front line with Russia.
Mr Rasmussen insisted that such a deployment would be in line with international rules as long as it was requested by Kyiv.
However, Mr Rasmussen’s ideas are likely to be controversial amongst Europe’s Nato allies.
Numerous countries have said they would not actively shoot down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory for fear of becoming a genuine party to the conflict.
Belgium has repeatedly blocked EU discussions about using a tranche of frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine’s defence.
While Germany has recently warned that it cannot donate any more Patriot interceptor missiles because it doesn’t have the stockpiles to defend its own country.
“Maybe Poland is in a different situation, but Germany, I don’t understand why they cannot deliver those Patriot systems. Deliver them now; they are needed right now in Ukraine… Germany is not threatened now,” Mr Rasmussen said.
The former Nato chief, who was involved in talks with Russia when it first invaded Ukraine’s Crimea peninsula in 2014, said the Continent was right to reopen communication channels with Moscow.
But he warned against linking discussions on a ceasefire in Ukraine to negotiations over a future European security architecture, arguing that Putin would seek to exploit the talks to restrict the military capabilities of both Kyiv and the alliance.
That said, Mr Rasmussen believes Nato could ultimately offer Russia security guarantees, given that its allies have no plans to attack Moscow.
“Why not? It wouldn’t cost anything to give such a security guarantee,” he concluded.

articles.title_orig: Singapore Says Warns Alice Huang, Lacks Evidence of Offenses
articles.title_zh: Singapore Says Warns Alice Huang, Lacks Evidence of Offenses
articles.content_orig:
Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have simultaneously owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, while she was in business with Nvidia and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang .
The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government.
This previously unreported entanglement was first uncovered by the research firm which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world. The connections may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown.
The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China.
Huawei is known as a Chinese government "state champion" in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government's push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party.
Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together in December 2023.
In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor , specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips.
"This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," said Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations.
If the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred "controlled equipment" to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said.
The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship.
Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached.
According to Chinese corporate records and media reports compiled by Tesari and provided to CNBC, Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le and who according to documents at the time was based in Hong Kong, in 2019 sold a cloud business she owned called Osmanthus to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road. A subsidiary of 7Road, which was based in Singapore, was spun off as "Megaspeed" in 2023 . Megaspeed would go on to become a key Nvidia customer, helping facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, The Information reported Tuesday.
As early as 2016, Alice Huang had also become a co-owner of a financial firm known as Shanghai Hexi , which heavily invests in tech and data centers.In 2021, Hexi in turn acquired 27 percent of a company called Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer, which Hexi held until 2024 . That firm owned a controlling 50.1 percent stake in a data center facility called Shenzhen Yifeng Technology Co., Ltd. in mainland China.
The key customer of that data center was Huawei Cloud , the Shenzhen, China-based subsidiary of Huawei Technologies.
In addition, Alice Huang's firm Hexi guaranteed the loans required to finance the Shenzhen data center, which did business with Huawei.
Hexi did not immediately respond to a message via its LinkedIn page sent outside of normal business hours.
CNBC translated corporate records and Chinese news articles in Mandarin that Tesari provided.
It's not clear if the Shenzhen data center was able to acquire Nvidia GPUs, but its majority owner began purchasing the chips in 2023 . That company is known as Zhejiang Century Huatong Group and is a business partner of Alice Huang's Hexi through their joint ownership of Century Longteng.
That made Alice Huang a part owner of a data center providing computing power to Huawei. And that was happening at around the same time the first known sightings came of Alice Huang and Jensen Huang in public together.
And that raises the question of why Huawei, which has access to Chinese made chips, would need to rent computing power from an outside entity.
Hexi exited its stake in the data center development company in 2024, but individuals within Alice Huang's network are still connected to the Shenzhen data center. Her husband Kang Wei is a longtime business associate who founded Hexi, where Alice Huang previously held an executive role. In 2022, Kang became an executive of Century Longteng, which owns the controlling stake in the Shenzhen data center and he also attended the company's signing of the Huawei agreement.

articles.title_orig: 'Big Short' Michael Burry says to 'get out' of Nvidia stock on CEO Jensen Huang's exit
articles.title_zh: 'Big Short' Michael Burry says to 'get out' of Nvidia stock on CEO Jensen Huang's exit
articles.content_orig:
Michael Burry says Jensen Huang 's exit will deal a heavy blow to Nvidia, and investors should sell their shares before the company hits the skids.
Huang resigned as the AI chipmaker's CEO on Thursday morning following fresh reports about two alleged extramarital affairs.
After it emerged on Wednesday that Nvidia's board was considering ousting Huang, Burry — who has been publicly betting against Nvidia for many months — laid out in a Substack post why he expected Nvidia to suffer without Huang in charge.
Huang has "orchestrated" Nvidia's efforts to expand the AI ecosystem, Burry wrote. He pointed to its huge investments in AI stocks, and its use of special vehicles and hidden debt to finance customers' purchases of its chips, creating "tremendous leverage in the system."
He also claimed that Huang pushed customers to buy chips they didn't need yet by threatening to reduce their allocations in the future.
Without Huang at Nvidia's helm, the "cash may cease to flow, " and investments could dry up or be written off, Burry wrote.
Customers will be free to "slow down deals, push back, renegotiate terms, or simply walk to a competitor without fear of offending" the chip chief , he continued.
"Nvidia's business will not disappear, but its growth may slow and, critically, its margins may fall," Burry added.
"The terms of trade and the architecture of financing were the secret sauce that supercharged an already dominant technology," he wrote, adding that it will "take time for this Byzantine web to untangle and unwind."
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
"Nvidia bulls will have another fluffy big chance to get out," Burry added. "Get out."
Nvidia stock plunged at the start of trading on Thursday and has seen a near-35% drop from its $ 243-per-share peak in early October.
Burry, who shot to fame after his prescient bet against the mid-2000s housing bubble was featured in the book and movie "The Big Short," pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments last year.
He's one of several commentators who soured on Nvidia in recent days.
Bernstein Research's Stacy Rasgon downgraded the stock to "Market Perform" and halved his price target to $200 in a research note before Huang's resignation.
In a Bloomberg TV interview, he warned of more bad press and regulatory scrutiny , questioned whether Nvidia could find a CEO as visionary as Huang, and flagged the risk of an employee exodus.
Oppenheimer's Rick Schafer downgraded Nvidia to "Perform" and removed his price target in a Wednesday research note.
He wrote that Huang plays a crucial role as the " face of AI ," his leadership has been "critical to Nvidia's success," and the company has " massive shoes to fill and no obvious successor."
He added that Huang's exit could spark a "brain drain" and result in a "lingering share overhang."
Nvidia's directors have appointed the company's finance chief, Colette Kress, as interim CEO while they search for a permanent replacement for Huang.

articles.title_zh: Israeli Strikes on Gaza Hospital Kill 6 and Injure Dozens, Health Officials Say
articles.content_orig:
The Israeli military struck a hospital in the southern Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing at least six people and injuring 28 more, according to local health officials.
Dr. Ahmed al-Farra, general director of Nasser Hospital, said in a news conference on Thursday that two missiles had hit the facility and that among the dead was Rezeq Abu Shaira, 52, a doctor.
Health officials reached in Gaza by phone said that a man called Khaled Abu Anza had also been killed. A spokeswoman for the Israeli military, speaking on condition of anonymity in line with protocol, said that Mr. Abu Anza was a Hamas operative.
The Israeli security agency and military said in a joint statement on Thursday that they had targeted Muhammad Abu Ismail, whom they identified as a Hamas commander “responsible for holding numerous hostages captive” during the Gaza war.
The Israeli authorities said that Hamas had established a command center at the hospital complex to stage operations against Israeli forces and was storing weapons there. They added that steps had been taken to mitigate harm to civilians.
Hamas said the Israeli claim that the hospital was used for military activity was a “blatant attempt to justify a heinous crime targeting a civilian medical facility.” Residents of Gaza have said that officials affiliated with Hamas-run Gaza government and security forces sometimes use the enclave’s hospitals as offices.

Schumer says the Trump administration also must answer for what it did once it learned about Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
Among the questions that need to be answered is what the president knew when he personally invited Huang aboard Air Force One on a state visit to Beijing earlier this year, Schumer said in his social media post on X.

The bill would allow them to collect all their retirement and disability pay, which the Congressional Budget Office has estimated would boost total compensation by an average of about $1,450 a month.

The Nasdaq Composite fluctuated on Thursday as investors assessed the departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , betting it would not derail the whole AI trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq was last down 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average traded around the flatline. The S&P 500 fell 0.1%.
Selling pressure on Nvidia eased a bit, with the stock last down 5%. The shares were down double digits at one point after the company announced that Huang had resigned and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. This comes after Huang reportedly had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Investors moved into competitors of Nvidia, including Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom , helping to bolster the market. AMD shares were up 4%, while Broadcom gained 5%.
Hyperscalers Microsoft and Alphabet — key buyers of Nvidia chips and leaders of the AI rally — also increased.
"This is a golden opportunity for Amazon, for Google, for AMD, for Broadcom, for OpenAI and Anthropic, who are hiring chip experts to help them design their own chips," said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management.
"Nvidia's fate as one company is one thing, but this AI revolution is way bigger than that," he also said. "If Nvidia falls from grace and their chips are no longer the best, and AMDs are better or Google's are better, then people will switch over and buy them. The demand for the chips is not is not going down."
There was a sense from investors that perhaps Huang's exit was a capitulation event for the AI trade with Nvidia's stock down by more than 25% the past one month as this scandal was unfolding.
"We are sticking with the thesis that technology stocks bottomed last week," said Tom Lee, the head of research at Fundstrat, in a note Thursday. Huang's departure "does not change our view."
Stocks outside of technology such as JPMorgan and Eli Lilly traded higher as well.
Stephanie Link said Thursday she sold her Nvidia following Jensen Huang's resignation from his post as CEO, with the investor moving into another artificial intelligence play: Micron Technology .
"The fundamentals are very, very strong at [Nvidia], and I expect the quarter next week to be very good with 300 billion in free cash flow next year," Link, the chief investment strategist at Hightower Advisors, said on CNBC's " Halftime Report ." "But, this stock is not going to trade on fundamentals ... for a while because you have the overhang of the investigations of leadership changes of potential departures."

Nvidia shares were trading down 4% on Thursday after Jensen Huang announced he would immediately step down as CEO and a member of the board at the chipmaker.

Paul Meeks says he's buying Nvidia shares with "both hands" despite CEO Jensen Huang's resignation , because the decline amid this unfolding scandal has brought the stock down to "stupid" valuation levels.
The Freedom Capital head of technology research noted that the stock is trading at just 10 times fiscal 2028 earnings estimates after Thursday's decline.
Nvidia shares are off 20% in November alone, pressured by the scandal unfolding.
"I think that the actual announcement of his resignation is a market-clearing event," said Meeks.
CNBC Pro subscribers can learn more about Meeks' other key points here .
Even as Nvidia shares remained lower following CEO Jensen Huang's resignation , the broader market rose as investors moved past the announcement.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite , both of which began Thursday's session lower, rose 0.2% and 0.1%, respectively.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average outperformed, rising 138 points, or 0.3%.
Sales of existing homes fell to their lowest level in more than 16 years during October, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday.
A decline of 5.5% brought the seasonally adjusted annualized rate down to 3.75 million during a month that saw mortgage rates continue to climb, putting pressure on an already beleaguered housing market. The total was the lowest since August 2010.
"Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," said NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun. "Based on the current underwhelming home sales pace at a time of consistent job growth, there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline."
Nvidia shares are seeing huge volume as the stock drops following the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang .
The chipmaker saw more than 373 million shares traded amid the selling pressure. That's above the stock's 30-day average of 144.4 million.
The stock was last down more than 5%.
Cleveland Federal Reserve President Beth Hammack said Thursday she doesn't see the need for aggressive interest rate increases ahead.
While Hammack still supports rate hikes as the Fed struggles to get inflation back to its 2% target, she advocated for a gradual approach that the economy can adapt to more easily.
"I think we need to move rates higher to get to a restrictive stance of policy to bring inflation back down to 2%. My view is that if we go steadily in smaller increments, more frequent, smaller rises, it's easier for businesses and households to manage around that," she sad. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements."
Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller raised the specter of a half-point hike at the December meeting if the inflation data comes in worse than anticipated. However, Hammack said she doesn't think that's necessary, at least for now.
"If we get behind the curve, and I don't think we're behind the curve today, but if we get behind the curve, then that might be something that we need to consider," she said. "So I'll certainly have an open mind walking into that December meeting."
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began Thursday's session in the red.
The broad market index fell 0.8% shortly after the opening bell, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq declined 1.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 108 points, or 0.2%.
Shares of Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices gained about 3% each in premarket trading after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia.
The company's chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim chief.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The General Staff called the refineries in Omsk, Kirish, Ryazan, Nizhny Novgorod and Yaroslavl “among the five most powerful in the country.”
According to figures cited by Ukrainian arms maker Fire Point , the targeted facilities have a combined refining capacity of over 120 million metric tons of crude per year, or about 36% of Russia’s total refining capacity.
The latest operations underscore Kyiv’s expanding ability to strike critical energy infrastructure deep inside Russian territory, placing facilities far beyond the immediate frontline within reach of Ukrainian long-range weapons.
In early July, Ukraine’s General Staff claimed to have knocked 43% of Russia’s refining capacity offline.
In early November, Russia introduced fuel sales restrictions in multiple regions following a brief respite in late October, coinciding with a brief pause in Ukrainian strikes due to US pressure.
On Nov. 11, Ukraine’s Special Operation Forces (SSO) said they struck the Omsk Oil refinery in Siberia for the third time, nearly 2,500 kilometers (around 1,550 miles) from the Ukrainian border, after earlier strikes in July and October .
The SSO described the refinery as Russia’s largest and one of its main producers of motor gasoline and aviation fuel. In a Nov. 6 post, it said the Omsk facility is the only Russian producer of catalysts used in secondary oil processing, meaning other refineries depend on its output.
The latest wave also hit several major refineries responsible for a major share of Russia’s petroleum production.
On Nov. 9, Ukrainian forces struck the Kirishi refinery , also known as KIFEF, in Russia’s Leningrad region. With an annual processing capacity of approximately 20 million metric tons, it accounts for more than 6% of the country’s total refining output.
Two days earlier, on Nov. 7, Ukraine targeted the Saratov Oil Refinery . The facility processes approximately 7 million metric tons of crude annually and supplies petroleum products to Russia’s industrial and military sectors.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Data Centers Will Continue to Be Built, Despite Midterm Elections
articles.title_zh: Data Centers Will Continue to Be Built, Despite Midterm Elections
articles.content_orig:
The already-wobbly artificial intelligence trade took another hit from the midterm elections, as investors reconsidered the outlook for the data center construction boom that has lifted many stocks. Despite the fresh headwind of uncertainty about what the Democratic Party midterm sweep will mean for the data center buildout, strategists say AI opportunities remain, but investors will need to be more selective.
A slowdown could offer the hyperscalers—Microsoft MSFT , Alphabet GOOG / GOOGL , Amazon AMZN , Meta Platforms META , and Oracle ORCL —greater pricing power, ease pressure on their cash flows, and enhance their structural advantage over neocloud competitors. The divide between haves and have-nots in the semiconductor industry could expand as data center developers seek to cram as much computing power as possible into each facility. Suppliers of ancillary services like power generation and cooling could face headwinds from a smaller data center footprint.
“Right now, the path of AI is unfortunately unknowable,” said Sameer Samana, head of global equities and real assets at the Wells Fargo Investment Institute, on a call with clients Friday. “The only thing I do know is it’ll be a more moderate pace than it used to be.”
AI has driven stock market gains for the better part of four years. Since the beginning of 2023, shortly after the release of ChatGPT, AI stocks have returned nearly twice as much as the broader market. In that time, the rally endured its fair share of setbacks, but last week’s was arguably the most punishing yet. Two days after the election, the Morningstar US Artificial Intelligence Index dropped more than 9%—its worst day since the onset of the covid-19 pandemic in March 2020. The index’s year-to-date return dropped into single digits last week for the first time since April.
The rout underscored the volatility of a highly concentrated and uncertain market, leaving investors wondering whether the panic was a hiccup, like prior AI selloffs, or the beginning of a new reality.
Last week’s slump was sparked by Democrats who campaigned against data centers getting elected to statewide offices in states with high concentrations of data centers, like Texas, Ohio, and Georgia. They ran on imposing moratoriums on new data center development and implementing more stringent regulations around electricity and water use. Investors fear opposition to data centers will slow their construction, softening demand for semiconductors, networking equipment, and other AI-enabling hardware.
Spending on data centers has energized the stock market and broader economy for years. The hyperscalers and SpaceX SPCX are expected to spend more than $900 billion on capital expenditures this year, nearly twice 2025’s total, which was itself nearly double 2024, according to JPMorgan. Their investments in AI-enabling infrastructure have helped companies outfit data centers with semiconductors, servers, networking equipment, and more. As a result, the fates of some of America’s most valuable companies, like Nvidia NVDA and Micron MU , are now inextricably linked to the data center boom.
Strategists say development may slow, but companies have options. Denny Fish, portfolio manager and lead technology equity analyst at Janus Henderson, says future data centers that might have broken ground in Texas may move to more hospitable states. He notes that on the same day tech stocks sold off, Alphabet announced a $17 billion data center project in Republican-led Wyoming. “This data center capacity will get shifted one way or another,” he says.
Companies also have plenty of incentives to aggressively pursue data center projects. “Every one of these CEOs and founders view this as existential,” says Fish. In addition, “at the federal level, this is non-optional.” The White House still considers American AI leadership a national security imperative.
All these factors give some strategists and money managers confidence that the AI buildout has plenty of runway. “We took advantage of the opportunity when things became dislocated as it relates to valuations,” says Marc Nabi, equity investment director at Capital Group. “Even though there might be near-term headwinds from a regulatory standpoint, the long-term opportunity of market share leaders should persist.”
One potential winner of slower data center construction: hyperscalers. “This really benefits the companies that have capital and have existing data center footprints,” says Janus Henderson’s Fish. Investors may have thought the same last week. The hyperscalers were mostly spared from Thursday’s carnage, and most of their stocks are up since the midterms.
Demand for computing capacity has exceeded supply for years, which has helped accelerate growth in hyperscalers’ cloud businesses. If moratoriums and harsher regulations slow the addition of new capacity, that supply/demand imbalance may be exacerbated. “Tighter constraints on compute capacity could support greater pricing power, higher incremental margins, and improving operating cash flow for hyperscalers,” wrote JPMorgan analysts in a note late last week.
Slower development could also ease pressure on hyperscalers’ free cash flows, which turned negative this year for the entire group except Microsoft. That cash burn has become a symbol of the data center buildout’s immense costs and uncertain returns, and a major drag on investor sentiment. It has also forced hyperscalers to sell debt and issue equity, increasing their interest rate risk and diluting shareholders.
After last week’s selloff, JPMorgan analysts “see attractive risk-reward” in hyperscaler stocks and “believe the group has room to re-rate higher over the medium term.”
Semiconductors were among the hardest-hit stocks during last week’s rout. The group had been in a slump since late June, following a blistering run-up in the second quarter. Thursday’s selloff deepened the pullback. The PHLX Semiconductor Index finished Thursday 37% below its June peak, 5 percentage points more than the average peak-to-trough drawdown in past boom/bust cycles, according to Vivek Arya, managing director and senior analyst at Bank of America.
After Thursday’s selloff, 63% of technology stocks were trading below their 200-day moving average—a key trendline analysts use to gauge a stock’s momentum. It was one of the worst readings on that front in years, close to “historical washout territory,” according to Darrell Cronk, president of the Wells Fargo Investment Institute.
Strategists say some babies have likely been thrown out with the bathwater. “The semiconductor ecosystem in general should remain relatively robust for several years, just given the supply-demand imbalances,” says Fish of Janus Henderson. But he predicts markets are “moving away from the rising tide lifts all boats [trend]” that characterized the chip rally earlier this year.
Fish says a data center slowdown would likely benefit the chipmakers with the most efficient hardware. If constructing data centers becomes more cumbersome, developers have an incentive to maximize their facility’s token output, which is a potential tailwind for technology leaders like Nvidia.
To be sure, all chipmakers with data center exposure would be impacted by a material slowdown. “It probably takes a little air out of the [earnings] estimates for 2028 and 2029,” says Fish.
BofA’s Arya estimates some of that air has already been let out. “Semis already trade at a 22% discount to the broader market,” he wrote last week, “suggesting a decent chunk of [EPS] cuts may already be reflected” in stock prices.
Strategists say the outlook is haziest for neoclouds like CoreWeave CRWV and Nebius NBIS , cloud computing upstarts constructing purpose-built AI data centers. Unlike hyperscalers, neoclouds have no existing businesses generating cash to funnel into data center construction. articles.title_orig: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.title_zh: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years, before hundreds of thousands join protest
articles.content_orig:
Madrid, Spain – Tens of thousands of young people have protested across Spain in recent weeks, rallying against the country’s acute housing crisis. On Wednesday, many have gone on strike, heeding calls by Spain’s biggest unions for a nationwide walkout under the slogan: “Salarios, vivienda y precios” – or “wages, housing, and prices”.
Anger grew last month after the forcible eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid flat where she had lived for the past seven decades. Her corporate landlord had raised the rent to a level above her means. As the public outcry worsened, she died in hospital the day the property owners who had evicted her agreed to allow her to return to her home.
To protect vulnerable renters, the government presented two emergency decrees to parliament, but these were defeated by right-wing parties.
Spain’s left-wing coalition government called a snap election for November 29, hoping to capitalise on anger over the housing crisis to rally voters as Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had trailed in the polls to the conservative People’s Party and the far-right Vox party.
Against this backdrop, the Bank of Spain has said the country has a shortage of 750,000 homes, but this figure could rise to 1 million by next year.
Al Jazeera spoke to several protesters about their demands:
Haris Javaid Sharif, 24, a data analyst, lives with his parents, brother and sister in a 44sq-metre (474-foot) flat in Barcelona. Sharif earns $1,900 per month net. The family pay $745 for their rented flat, of which he pays half. He still lives with his parents as average rental prices for a three-bedroom flat in Barcelona range between $954 and $1,684.
“After the pandemic, we were evicted from our flat because we owed five months rent. My father and I could not work because of the pandemic. When we got the 2,500 euros ($2,800), the owner did not want to negotiate and we lost our home.
“We went 11 months without work and we lived in two-room accommodation. I thought it only happens to vulnerable people, but it can happen to anyone.
“I still live with my parents as housing is so expensive. I am joining the strike to try to press these politicians. The housing problems for youngsters is the biggest problem. I speak to people who don’t see themselves buying a house in 10 years’ time.”
Bea Garcia de la Torre, 32, who works for a foundation in Madrid, shares a 70sq-metre (753sq-foot) flat with her brother. They pay $1,229 per month in rent. She earns $2,400 per month.
“I am not in the worst position. There are some people who have to pay half their monthly wages in rent. My brother and I share the rent, but the landlord is trying to get us to pay for the central heating, which is something which should be paid for by the community. We are also worried that he might put up the rent to an astronomical amount or kick us out.
“I will join this general strike because it is a good chance to change the housing policy in this country, just like we did with a similar action and won the right to an eight-hour day.”
Iratxe Gonzalez, 27, a social worker, shares a flat in Madrid with three other people. She earns $1,200 per month, of which she pays $400 in rent for the flat of 45sq metres (484sq foot).
“I needed to leave my parents’ home, but the flat is very small, and we only have a short-term contract of one year. It is not very secure. The landlord could push up the rent or just get rid of us. I feel this is an issue which is important for every young person in Spain right now.”
Ignacio Redrado, a 32-year-old teacher who could only afford to leave home when he was 26, earns $2,245 and pays $337 in rent per month. He shares a cramped flat in Madrid with four others, which measures 60 sq metres (646sq feet). They pay $1,067 per month in rent. Madrid has the highest rental prices in Spain, with an average flat for four people costing between $2,500 and $6,737.
“The average for leaving home in Spain is 30 years old. We have called a general strike because we cannot take any more. We must act. It is not about this government. The power should be with the people. We must solve the problem of housing. We want indefinite rental contracts and more social housing.”
Arturo Leon, 24, works with an NGO and hopes to study for a doctorate in housing justice. He shares a small flat in Barcelona with four others and pays $506 per month in rent.
“We do not have a contract, and there are lots of things in the flat which are broken, but the landlord refuses to fix. My bedroom measures only two metres by 2.6 metres (6.6 feet by 8.5 feet). But despite this, the landlord is threatening to put up the rent. This is a perfect example of why I will be joining the general strike.”

articles.title_orig: Singapore barred Alice Huang for giving police ‘inaccurate information’
articles.title_zh: Singapore barred Alice Huang for giving police ‘inaccurate information’
articles.content_orig:
Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang .
Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.
The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government.
In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had been uncooperative. Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe.
Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.
Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.”
“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said.
Supermicro did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”
She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.
Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

articles.title_orig: Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
articles.title_zh: Indonesia's VP resigns as his eligibility and academic credentials are questioned
articles.content_orig:
Indonesian Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka leaves the parliament building after submitting his resignation letter in Jakarta, Indonesia, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. Tatan Syuflana/AP hide caption
JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president resigned on Thursday as questions grew over his eligibility for the office after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, submitted his resignation to the leadership of the People's Consultative Assembly, the country's highest legislative body, at the parliament building in the capital, Jakarta.
Raka didn't comment as he left the meeting.
"There will always be political dynamics in public office, that's normal," his father, Widodo, told reporters from his hometown in Solo, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.
"We will continue to support President Prabowo's government, especially programs that serve the interests of the broader public," he said, referring to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto.
The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to investigations into allegations that top police officials had been involved in wiretapping targeting the president.
Raka had offered to resign Tuesday during a meeting with Prabowo, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy. He personally delivered his resignation letter to the president on Wednesday.
Prabowo addressed the nation Thursday afternoon after holding a meeting with Raka and the parliamentary leadership at the presidential palace.
Flanked by Raka and top leaders of parliament, a grim-looking Prabowo said that he accepted Raka's resignation "with a heavy heart" and praised the vice president for showing "courage, responsibility and statesmanship" by stepping down.
"He chose to resign for the greater interest of the nation, the state and the Indonesian people," Prabowo said in a televised statement. "He has been a great help to me, from our election campaign through the past two years of government. Many of our achievements would not have been possible without his contribution."
Prabowo praised Raka's dedication and hard work, highlighting Raka's visits to 35 provinces and 149 regencies and cities to inspect 303 government projects during the past two years as examples of his commitment to public service.
"I will continue to support him, and I pray that he and his family are given strength during what is undoubtedly a difficult time," Prabowo said.
Under the Indonesian Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy doesn't trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People's Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents that Raka submitted regarding his overseas education didn't meet election requirements.
A subsequent petition, submitted Wednesday to the House leadership by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties, began a parliamentary process that could have led to his impeachment.
The push for his impeachment was driven largely by long-running allegations that Raka's candidacy was enabled by a Constitutional Court ruling that critics see as a conflict of interest and evidence of weak political accountability and dynastic privilege.
Before Prabowo chose him as his running mate for the 2024 election, Raka didn't meet the age requirement of 40 for vice presidential candidates. But the court's contentious ruling in October 2023 carved an exception allowing those who served or had been elected as regional leaders to run at a younger age.
Under Indonesian election law, a presidential or vice-presidential candidate must have completed senior high school or an equivalent level of education. Because Raka completed his secondary education overseas, he was required to provide documents showing that his qualifications were equivalent to an Indonesian high school diploma.
Raka was the first vice president of the country to resign before the end of a term since the fall of dictator Suharto and the start of Indonesia's democratic reforms in 1998.
Parliamentary leaders were due to convene immediately to begin the process of selecting a replacement, Speaker Ahmad Muzani said.
"We ask for the prayers and support of all Indonesians so that this democratic process can proceed smoothly and serve as a constructive new precedent in our constitutional system," Muzani told reporters.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine peace talks: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff conclude talks with Putin
articles.title_zh: Ukraine peace talks: Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff conclude talks with Putin
articles.content_orig:
Below is a roundup of developments from the Ukraine-Russia talks on Thursday, November 12:
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have concluded meetings with Russian President Vladimir Putin and will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy who is attending a European summit there.
Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, described talks with Putin as "substantive and detailed."
He and Witkoff were in Moscow after two-days of talks in Abu Dhabi seeking to find a way to end Russia's ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
In Moscow, however, Putin showed no inclination toward compromise, saying that he would no back off of his territorial demands, while at the same time rejecting proposals to station foreign peacekeeping troops in  Ukraine, dismissing such a deployment as a "continuation of war."
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed their trip to Abu Dhabi this week with Russian President Vladimir Putin .
According to Russian state media RIA Novosti, Witkoff said US President Donald Trump was "seeking to end the conflict in Ukraine as quickly as possible."
The three-way talks in Abu Dhabi between the US, Ukraine and Russia were held "in a positive atmosphere" and that the Ukrainian and Russian delegations had "worked effectively," Ria Novosti reported.
Witkoff said he would convey the results of his and Kushner's meeting with Putin to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy .
Kushner, for his part, said the US had begun discussions with European countries on the post-war "security architecture" on the continent.
He also said Europe wanted to be involved in the talks to end the conflict, RIA Novosti reported.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has proposed a "humanitarian mission" to the frontline city of Kostyantynivka in eastern Ukraine, Russian state media reported.
Putin made the remarks during a meeting at the Kremlin on Thursday with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Ria Novosti said.
"There's a village in Donbas called Kostyantynivka, where there are still about 400-500 civilians. Let's do the same thing we did in Oleshky and invite representatives of the foreign press, including the American press," he said, referring to the recent US-brokered evacuation of the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine .
According to RIA Novosti, Putin also repeated Russia's demands in a potential peace deal, including its refusal to accept any foreign troops in Ukraine.
The Russian leader warned that international peacekeepers in Ukraine would become a "legitimate target for the Russian army."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the Russian side is becoming more willing to accept a European seat in the trilateral talks.
Merz said he expected Putin to agree to Europeans getting a seat at the table in talks with Ukraine. He was speaking on the sidelines of the European Political Community meeting in Dublin. He added that getting Putin to negotiate is more important than naming who would be the European envoy.
"The important thing is that Russia comes to the table and that Russia is ready to talk," the German chancellor said.
He also highlighted Ukraine's importance to Europe, saying that supporting Kyiv was a "shared European responsibility."

Hi! I’m Jen Tuohy, The Verge’s senior smart home reviewer. I’ve tested every smart display Amazon and Google have ever made, and for the past week I’ve been testing Apple’s first: The $299 HomeView.
I put the tabletop and wall-mounted versions through their paces, on my kitchen counter, bedside table, in my office, and on my coffee table. I also mounted one as a smart home control panel in my entryway. I cooked with it, ran my smart home from it, took calls on it, and tested its new Siri AI capabilities.
I also let my family loose on it, and my tech-averse husband was a big fan. My teenage daughter, less so. (Ask me why).
Verge subscribers can submit questions starting right now in the comments, and I’ll start answering later today at 2PM ET / 11AM PT.

articles.title_orig: The new Apple TV 4K is great, but expensive
articles.title_zh: The new Apple TV 4K is great, but expensive
articles.content_orig:
The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K is pricey at $300, but its hands-free Siri, blazing A19 performance, and ad-free tvOS interface make it the best premium media streamer you can buy.
The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K finally adds hands-free Siri and gets a major speed boost from the iPhone 17's A19 chip. It also costs $299, $170 more than its 2022 predecessor. That's a steep jump, though nearly every media streamer has gotten pricier this year as component costs have climbed. What you get for the money is the fastest streamer I've tested, running tvOS, the cleanest and most polished streaming platform available, with none of the ads or pushy recommendations that clutter competitors' platforms . It's also a capable smart home hub with Matter support, a FaceTime machine that uses your iPhone as a webcam, and, with two pairs of HomePods, the heart of a wireless surround-sound system. Cheaper alternatives abound, but the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K is the best premium media streamer you can buy, earning it our Editors' Choice award.
I thought the $129 third-generation Apple TV 4K was too expensive when I reviewed it four years ago, so the new model's $300 price seemed absurd at first, even with its upgrades. Then I tested it, and its speed, hands-free Siri, and ad-free interface changed my mind.
Still, if $300 is more than you want to spend, there are strong alternatives. The Roku Ultra ($149.99) also offers hands-free voice control and a streamlined, media-forward interface, though it lacks a full AI assistant and the Apple TV 4K's extensive smart home features. The Amazon Fire TV Cube ($199.99) has hands-free Alexa+ and is an even more powerful smart home hub, but its interface is clunky and full of ads, and it doesn't support AirPlay. And if you don't need hands-free voice control at all, streaming sticks like the Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Plus ($69.99) and the Roku Streaming Stick Plus ($59.99) add streaming to any TV for well under $100.
The new Apple TV 4K looks just like its predecessor: a black, rounded square box measuring 3.7 by 1.2 inches (width by height). The front has a status LED, and the back has HDMI, Ethernet, and power-cable ports.
The remote is also unchanged on the outside. It's a slim aluminum bar that feels more like a narrow iPhone than a typical streaming remote. Near the top is a large navigation pad with a circular center button that doubles as a touchpad. Above the pad sit the power button and a pinhole microphone, and a Siri button runs along the right edge. The rest of the controls are minimal: a volume rocker, a mute button, a play/pause button, a back button (long-press it to return to the home screen), and an Apple TV button, which opens the Apple TV app with a press and a quick settings menu with a long press. A built-in rechargeable battery charges over USB-C on the bottom.
The remote looks and feels great in the hand, but it can occasionally be frustrating to use. The touchpad is overly sensitive, and I’ve repeatedly brushed against it while pressing the directions around it, throwing off what I was trying to select. You can turn off the touchpad, but that raises the question of whether it was necessary to begin with. It can be useful when you want to swipe through multiple items at once, but I ended up turning it off anyway. I also kept mistaking the Apple TV button for the Home button until I found a setting that made it one. With those two tweaks, the remote became much easier to use.
Internally, the remote has a new trick: Precision Finding. If you have an iPhone 17 or later, an iPhone Air , or an iPhone Duo , you can use the Find My app to locate the remote to within about two feet. You can also use your phone to activate a chime on the remote to find it more easily.
The Apple TV 4K gets a major hardware boost from the A19 chip, the same processor that powers the iPhone 17 , along with 8GB of memory. That's a big jump from the previous model's A15 Bionic (from the iPhone 13 ) and 4GB of memory. Media streamers don't need nearly as much processing power as phones or tablets, but extra headroom makes them more responsive when you jump between apps or play 4K HDR content. It also makes the Apple TV 4K a better gaming machine, since dozens of Apple Arcade titles run on tvOS.
Wireless connectivity also gets a bump on the new Apple TV 4K. It has Wi-Fi 7 , enabling 6GHz band connections and future-proofing it considerably compared with the third-generation’s Wi-Fi 6. Gigabit Ethernet is built-in if you want a wired network link. It also features Bluetooth 6.0 compared with the previous model’s Bluetooth 5.0.
For all that new tech, the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K’s media capabilities are the same as its predecessor's. It plays 4K video, including high dynamic range ( HDR ) content in Dolby Vision, HDR10, and HDR10+, and supports Dolby Atmos spatial audio . That covers just about every format you'll encounter.
Speaking of spatial audio, the Apple TV 4K has a neat new trick if you own second-generation HomePods or HomePod mini 2s . Earlier models let you connect a stereo pair of HomePods, which already sounds better than most TV speakers. The fourth-generation model lets you add a second pair, placing four HomePods as front-left, front-right, rear-left, and rear-right speakers for surround sound. With HomePod minis, you get 4.0-channel surround. With full-size HomePods, whose multiple directional drivers can bounce sound around the room, you get a full spatial audio sound field, including height effects.
It's similar to Fire TV's Alexa Home Theater , which pairs multiple Echo Dot Max or Echo Studio speakers with a compatible Fire TV device. I'm still testing the feature and will cover it in more detail in a separate story, but so far, setup has been smooth.
For the first few iterations of the Apple TV, I lamented its limited selection of apps and services, but the device has come a long way in recent years. Apple has polished its tvOS platform to a shine, making for an impressively elegant, smooth, and full-featured media streaming experience.
The interface is built around big, friendly tiles, with a simple home screen that holds six apps in a macOS dock-like bar at the bottom, and a larger contextual view that shows art or content suggestions based solely on the selected app. Scrolling down brings you to the full selection of apps on the device, and you can organize them into folders. It’s easy to understand, simple to navigate, and has no ads whatsoever. It’s everything I like about Roku’s devices, but even more polished.
For streaming, tvOS covers all major services including Apple TV (obviously), Amazon Prime Video , Crunchyroll, Disney+, Netflix, Twitch, and YouTube. You can also mirror your iPhone, iPad, or Mac screen to it over AirPlay. For local media servers, Plex has an official tvOS app, while Emby and Jellyfin have a slew of third-party apps but no official ones; I had no problem connecting to my Jellyfin server with several of them.
I want to give particular credit to the Twitch app on tvOS as the most responsive version I’ve used on a media streamer. On multiple Fire TV and Google TV devices I've tested, the Twitch app lags several seconds when backing out of a channel to the main app screen. On the Apple TV 4K, it’s instant. It's a small thing, but as a Twitch watcher, I appreciate it.
If you like to game, you can pair a Bluetooth gamepad to the Apple TV 4K to play. The selection is overwhelmingly mobile-focused, with the same kinds of games you would find on iPad, but there are still some great console-like picks like Dead Cells, PowerWash Simulator, and SpongeBob SquarePants: Battle for Bikini Bottom.
Apple Arcade extends to tvOS, too, though I didn’t see many stand-out gamepad games on it besides the aforementioned PowerWash Simulator. A Steam Link client is also available, so you can stream games from your PC to your TV. Thanks to the A19 chip, games play very smoothly.
OK, the Apple TV 4K isn’t going
